title: An Aubry-André localized optical lattice clock
authors: Shuo Ma, Anke Stölzel, Bennett Christensen, Zhuoli Ding, Dhruva Ganapathy, Andrew Householder, Genyue Liu, Shimon Kolkowitz
abstract: Optical lattice clocks in space could improve satellite navigation systems and enable new tests of fundamental physics, including gravitational-wave detection and tests of relativity. In microgravity, atoms can tunnel to degenerate neighboring lattice sites, broadening the clock transition and limiting coherence times. We demonstrate Aubry-André localization in a bichromatic optical lattice formed by two magic-wavelength lasers, suppressing tunneling in a horizontal lattice clock emulating free fall. We recover a Fourier-limited clock Rabi spectrum and measure Ramsey coherence times of up to 2 s in shallow lattices, with up to 100-fold improvement over the delocalized regime. These results establish Aubry-André localization as a practical route to controlling tunneling in future space-based clocks, and open a path to operating terrestrial clocks at shallower lattice depths.
summary: This paper presents a method to stabilize optical lattice clocks for space applications by inducing Aubry-André localization using a secondary lattice. By controlling the quasiperiodic potential, the technique suppresses detrimental atomic tunneling, which otherwise broadens the clock transition and limits coherence. This establishes AA localization as a practical tool for next-generation, high-precision quantum sensors.
main_problem: Operating high-precision optical lattice clocks in space requires suppressing atomic tunneling to maintain long coherence times, which is challenging in microgravity.
main_result: The authors demonstrated that implementing Aubry-André localization using a secondary lattice can suppress tunneling, recovering a narrow, Fourier-limited clock spectrum and achieving coherence times up to 2 s.
method: The study combines theoretical modeling of the Aubry-André Hamiltonian with experimental measurements of Rabi spectra and Ramsey coherence times.
model_or_system: The system is an optical lattice clock using $^{87}	ext{Sr}$ atoms in a bichromatic lattice formed by two magic-wavelength lasers. The physics is governed by the Aubry-André Hamiltonian, which models the interplay between nearest-neighbor tunneling and quasiperiodic on-site energy modulation.
key_observables: Rabi spectra (FWHM), Ramsey coherence times ($	au$), and the degree of spectral narrowing upon localization.
important_parameters: Secondary lattice depth ($\Delta$), tunneling matrix element ($J$), and the ratio of lattice wavelengths ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often approximates the incommensurate potential using a periodic supercell, and coherence time modeling relies on empirical fits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectral broadening in shallow single lattices versus the recovery of a narrow spectrum when a secondary lattice induces AA localization, alongside measurements of coherence time decay.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to suppress tunneling in space-based clocks, demonstrating the AA localization effect via spectral measurements, and finally modeling systematic shifts like hyperpolarizability and line pulling in the resulting superlattice.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major technological hurdle in quantum sensing by providing a robust, non-invasive method (AA localization) to control quantum coherence in a highly sensitive platform (optical lattice clocks).
